JSON: Name: anellovirus_earlylife_causal_pipeline Title: Longitudinal causal-integrative modeling of infant gut anellovirus dynamics to quantify effects of early-life exposures on childhood atopic disease Short Hypothesis: Attending daycare before 12 months causally reduces fecal anellovirus abundance and phylogenetic diversity at age one, and this reduction mediates a lower risk of allergic rhinitis by age six. Related Work: Metagenomic profiling studies have characterized the infant gut virome and identified high inter-individual anellovirus diversity and prevalence, with some cross-sectional links to birth mode, breastfeeding, and host FUT2 secretor status. Prior analyses have largely used univariate or standard multivariate association tests (PERMANOVA, GLMs) and machine-learning classifiers (random forest, PLS) to associate virome composition with exposures and outcomes. Limitations in existing work include small sample sizes or single-cohort analyses, limited taxonomic resolution or reliance on read-level mappings that underrepresent novel species, sparse consideration of compositional data properties, amplification biases in virome library preparation (e.g., MDA), minimal integration with host genotype and bacteriome, and a near absence of formal causal inference or mediation analysis to distinguish direct exposure effects from mediated effects via the virome. Few studies use validated counterfactual methods (IPW, marginal structural models, g-computation) or sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding, and replication across independent cohorts is uncommon. Abstract: We propose a reproducible pipeline that integrates metagenomic virome assembly, compositional statistics, multivariable prediction, and explicit causal inference to quantify how early-life social exposures alter infant gut anellovirus composition and whether those shifts mediate later allergic rhinitis. Using the deep COPSAC virome and matched bacterial 16S and host-genotype data, the pipeline standardizes contig-level vOTU clustering into species/subgenus, applies compositional transforms, and computes diversity and abundance metrics. Exposure effects (e.g., daycare, older siblings, FUT2 secretor) on anellovirus endpoints will be estimated with adjusted mixed models and validated via inverse-probability-weighted marginal structural models. Mediation analysis will quantify the proportion of exposure effect on allergic rhinitis explained by anellovirus metrics. Predictive models will compare virome-only, bacteriome-only, and integrated omics performance. The main contribution is a benchmarked, causally framed analysis workflow that yields interpretable effect estimates, mediation quantification, and robustness diagnostics. Expected outcomes are reproducible causal effect estimates and clarified mechanistic hypotheses linking social exposures, infant anelloviruses, and childhood atopic disease. Experiments: Primary datasets: COPSAC infant faecal virome sequencing (n=647 at 12 months, PRJEB46943), matched 16S bacterial profiles (n≈611, PRJNA417357), and host genotypes for FUT2 (rs601338) and clinical outcomes to age 6 (asthma, atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis). Secondary dataset for replication: available public infant virome cohort with ≥100 samples and matching clinical metadata (if available). Preprocessing: assemble contigs and deduplicate at 95% ANI to produce vOTUs; assign species/subgenus via whole-genome ANI tree cut; compute relative abundance and apply centred-log-ratio transform with pseudocount; filter taxa prevalence <5% for species analyses and <30% for predictive models. Baselines: (1) univariate GLMs adjusted for covariates; (2) PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis/Jaccard; (3) standard random forest and sPLS models for prediction; (4) compositional vs raw-abundance pipelines. Primary analysis: exposure = daycare start before sample; mediators = total anellovirus relative abundance and Faith's PD at 12 months; outcome = allergic rhinitis by age 6. Fit multivariable linear mixed models (random intercept for sequencing lane/batch, fixed covariates: age at sampling, sequencing depth, season, birth mode, antibiotics, breastfeeding, maternal atopy) to estimate exposure→mediator. Fit marginal structural model using inverse probability-of-treatment weighting to estimate exposure→outcome, then perform counterfactual mediation (g-computation or sequential g-estimation) to estimate mediated proportion and ATE with bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 replicates). Predictive experiments: 80/20 stratified cross-validation repeated 10 times; compare AUC, precision-recall, and R2 for models using (a) virome only, (b) bacteriome only, (c) combined virome+bacteriome, and (d) clinical covariates only. Ablation studies: (i) remove bacteriophage reads to test compositional shifts; (ii) species-level vs subgenus-level features; (iii) stratify by FUT2 secretor status; (iv) compare CLR vs raw relative abundance and vs presence/absence. Statistical thresholds: report FDR-adjusted p<0.05; report effect sizes, R2, ATE, and mediated proportion with CIs. Sensitivity analyses: E-value computation for unmeasured confounding, alternative covariate sets, and negative-control outcomes (e.g., unrelated health endpoint). Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical biases from multiple-displacement amplification and library preparation can distort viral relative abundances and species detection, producing measurement error in vOTU abundance and diversity. Sparse and zero-inflated taxa (low-prevalence species) reduce power and inflate false positives; compositional constraints can produce spurious correlations if transforms are misapplied. Single-timepoint virome data limits causal interpretation of temporal mediation; reverse causation or time-varying confounding may violate assumptions of marginal structural models. Residual confounding from unmeasured social or environmental variables (e.g., unrecorded infections, household contacts) can bias causal estimates; E-values and sensitivity tests cannot fully guarantee identifiability. Cohort-specific sample collection timing, storage, and sequencing batches may limit generalization; replication cohorts may be scarce. Host genetic interactions (FUT2) are underpowered if non-secretor frequency is low. Assembly and clustering at species/subgenus resolution are sensitive to reference completeness and may misclassify novel anelloviruses. Computational requirements for assembly, ANI calculations, and bootstrap mediation (large replicate counts) are substantial and may limit scalability. Predictive models may overfit given high dimensionality relative to sample size, yielding optimistic AUCs unless rigorously cross-validated.
